title: US Data centers are on the ballot
gist: Oxford Economics argues the November 2026 midterms matter for the US data center buildout mainly through gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia and Ohio rather than Congress, with a Democratic sweep raising odds of federal rules making data centers pay more of grid costs. It keeps its baseline unchanged, citing national security and bipartisan lobbying, and suggests moratorium threats may be pulling construction forward into 2026.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics says a Democratic sweep in the 2026 US midterms would raise the prospects of federal legislation forcing data centers to contribute more to grid costs and improve environmental reporting, while federal action would be more limited under a split Congress.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A Democratic sweep is a tail risk for hyperscaler power-cost economics via grid cost allocation, not an outright buildout halt.
insights.quote: A Democratic sweep in the midterms would raise the prospects of federal legislation to ensure data centers contribute more to grid costs and improve environmental reporting.
insights.locator: A Democratic sweep in the midterms

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues gubernatorial races matter much more than congressional outcomes for the US data center buildout, singling out Texas, Georgia and Ohio as the key states.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Investors tracking data center/power capex risk should watch state-level governor races in TX, GA and OH more than control of Congress.
insights.quote: The outcome of gubernatorial races matters much more for the data center buildout, especially in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio.
insights.locator: The outcome of gubernatorial races matters

insights.claim: Oxford Economics identifies simultaneous tightening of data center policy across the US South and Midwest as the main downside risk to the buildout, but notes local opposition mostly relocates projects rather than stopping them.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Local backlash is a site-selection reallocation story (winners/losers by state) unless it becomes coordinated across regions.
insights.quote: local opposition mostly relocates projects rather than stopping them
insights.locator: The outcome of gubernatorial races matters

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects the US political debate over data centers to intensify heading into the 2028 presidential election regardless of the 2026 midterm outcome.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Regulatory overhang on AI infrastructure is a multi-year theme, not a one-off election event.
insights.locator: A Democratic sweep in the midterms

insights.claim: According to Oxford Economics, opposition to data centers softens appreciably when projects deliver local benefits or supply their own power, and national security concerns plus bipartisan lobbying should limit the bite of future regulation, so it is not changing its baseline forecast despite rising political backlash.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Favors behind-the-meter / self-supplied power models and projects with local benefit packages; regulatory headlines may be overpriced as a threat.
insights.quote: Data center opposition softens appreciably when projects deliver local benefits or supply their own power.

themes.theme: Macro impact of AI capex timing

insights.claim: Oxford Economics suggests the threat of moratoriums and tougher rules may be pulling US data center construction forward into 2026, and even if such rules materialize after the midterms they would not immediately end AI capex's boost to GDP.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: 2026 construction strength may partly be regulatory front-running, implying a flatter 2027 profile than extrapolation suggests.
insights.quote: The threat of moratoriums and tougher rules may be pulling data center construction forward into this year.
insights.locator: The threat of moratoriums and tougher

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues that over the longer term a slower US data center buildout would not necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Implies the AI buildout pace carries macro costs (e.g., grid/resource strain) that a slowdown could ease, against the consensus that slower AI capex is purely negative.
insights.quote: Longer term, a slower buildout wouldn’t necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy.
insights.locator: The threat of moratoriums and tougher
